## Getting Started

Astryx requires **React 19** or later (`react` and `react-dom` are peer dependencies of `@astryxdesign/core`).

Install Astryx, a theme, and its peer dependencies:

```bash
# npm
npm install @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @stylexjs/stylex
npm install -D @astryxdesign/cli

# pnpm
pnpm add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @stylexjs/stylex
pnpm add -D @astryxdesign/cli

# yarn
yarn add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @stylexjs/stylex
yarn add -D @astryxdesign/cli
```

You can also install the CLI once for your computer, so `astryx` works in any folder and every coding agent knows Astryx; in a project, it still runs that project's own version:

```bash
npm i -g @astryxdesign/cli
```

Project install, global install, or both? `astryx docs global/project-global-or-both` compares them (both is recommended), and `astryx docs global` explains how global mode works.

The simplest setup is a few CSS imports plus a theme provider — no build plugin, no PostCSS or Babel config. See the **[@astryxdesign/core README](packages/core/README.md#quick-start)** for the full guide (Next.js, Tailwind, Vite, and CDN).

For reliable CLI access, add a script to your `package.json`:

```json
"scripts": {
  "astryx": "node node_modules/@astryxdesign/cli/clients/cli/bin/astryx.mjs"
}
```

Then use it as `npm run astryx -- component --list`. This avoids path errors when AI assistants or new developers invoke the CLI directly.

### Safe Adoption of Modern Features

* **Progressive Enhancement & Nuanced Fallbacks**: We distinguish between purely additive enhancements (like speculative preloading) which are safe to let older browsers silently ignore, and critical behaviors (like dialog controls or network beacons) where we write highly considered, low-overhead fallbacks.
* **Responsible Fallbacks**: We prioritize lightweight, case-specific custom fallbacks (<50 LOC) or conditionally-loaded polyfills instead of heavy third-party bundles.
* **Gotchas & Quirks**: We document hidden platform limitations, such as the 64KB payload quota for `fetchLater()` or macOS-specific scrollbar behaviors.
* **Baseline-Aware Integration**: We leverage real-time compatibility data from the **Baseline** project so agents dynamically adapt to current browser support.
* **Origin Trial & Volatile Feature Gates**: Guides covering experimental **Origin Trial** APIs or **volatile features** (single-engine features shipped within the last 3 months or still stabilizing) remain discoverable via `search`, but are gated on `retrieve` so agents do not adopt unstable APIs without explicit developer consent.

## Hard rules

- Never modifies source code itself. The only writes go to `plans/`; executors edit only in disposable worktrees, and merging is always yours.
- Never runs commands that mutate your working tree — read, search, and read-only analysis only.
- Never reproduces secret values. Locations and credential types only, rotation always recommended.
- Asked to implement? It declines and points at the plan (or offers `execute`).

## Invocation variants

- Bare invocation → full workflow above.
- `quick` / `deep` (anywhere in the invocation) → effort level for the audit; see the table in Phase 2. Composes with everything: `quick security`, `deep --issues`. Default is `standard`.
- With a focus argument (e.g. `security`, `perf`, `tests`) → run Recon, then audit only that category, then plan.
- `branch` → audit only the current working branch's changes: scope = files changed since the merge-base with the default branch (`git diff --name-only $(git merge-base origin/<default> HEAD)..HEAD`) plus their direct importers/callers. Light recon, all categories, usually no subagents. **Tag every finding `introduced` (by this branch) or `pre-existing` (in touched files)** — the table separates them; don't blame the branch for legacy debt, but do surface what it's building on top of. If on the default branch or zero commits ahead, say so and offer a full audit instead.
- `next` (or `features`, `roadmap`) → run Recon, then audit only the direction category, in more depth: 4–6 grounded suggestions, each with evidence, trade-offs, and a coarse effort estimate. Selected ones become design/spike plans, not build-everything plans.
- `plan <description>` → skip the audit; the user already knows what they want. Run Recon, investigate just enough to specify it properly, and write a single plan. If the description is too ambiguous to specify honestly, first try to resolve each ambiguity from the codebase itself; only what's left becomes questions to the user — asked one at a time, each with a recommended answer.
- `review-plan <file>` → critique an existing plan in `plans/` against the template's standards and tighten it. If you authored the plan in this same session, also have a fresh-context subagent read it cold and report ambiguities — self-critique misses gaps you mentally fill from context the executor won't have.
- `execute <plan>` → dispatch a cheaper executor subagent on one plan (isolated worktree), then review its diff like a tech lead — re-run done criteria, check scope, read the code — and render a verdict. Treat the executor's diff as untrusted until reviewed: verify every hunk traces to a plan step and reject any out-of-scope change, however plausible it looks. Requires a host agent that can spawn subagents in an isolated worktree; if yours can't, say so and hand the plan over for manual execution instead. **Read [references/closing-the-loop.md](references/closing-the-loop.md) before the first dispatch.**
- `reconcile` → process what happened since last session: verify DONE plans, investigate BLOCKED ones, refresh drifted TODOs, retire dead findings. See [references/closing-the-loop.md](references/closing-the-loop.md).
- `--issues` (modifier on any planning invocation) → also publish each written plan as a GitHub issue via `gh`, URL recorded in the plan and index. Only with the explicit flag. **Before creating any issue, check whether the repo is public (`gh repo view --json visibility`). If it is, warn the user that issues are publicly visible and get explicit confirmation before publishing any plan that describes a security vulnerability, credential location, or other sensitive finding.** See [references/closing-the-loop.md](references/closing-the-loop.md).

## Commands

9 slash commands that map to the development lifecycle. Each one activates the right skills automatically.

| What you're doing | Command | Key principle |
|-------------------|---------|---------------|
| Define what to build | `/spec` | Spec before code |
| Plan how to build it | `/plan` | Small, atomic tasks |
| Build incrementally | `/build` | One slice at a time |
| Prove it works | `/test` | Tests are proof |
| Set the quality bar | `/constraints` | Decide it once, enforce it everywhere |
| Review before merge | `/review` | Improve code health |
| Audit web performance | `/webperf` | Measure before you optimize |
| Simplify the code | `/code-simplify` | Clarity over cleverness |
| Ship to production | `/ship` | Faster is safer |

In Claude Code these install as plugin commands. Where a built-in command has the same name, as `/review` does, use the namespaced form: `/agent-skills:review`.

Want fewer manual steps once the spec exists? **`/build auto`** generates the plan and implements every task in a single approved pass — you approve the plan once, then it runs autonomously. It removes the human stepping *between* tasks, not the verification: every task is still test-driven and committed individually, and it pauses on failures or risky steps.

Skills also activate automatically based on what you're doing — designing an API triggers `api-and-interface-design`, building UI triggers `frontend-ui-engineering`, and so on.

# agent-browser Browser automation for AI agents: open pages, read them as an accessibility tree, and act on elements from the shell.

agent-browser is a native Rust CLI that gives an AI agent a browser it can drive one command at a time. `snapshot` returns the page as compact text with a ref such as `@e1` for each element. The agent acts on a ref, reads the page again to check the result, and repeats. The browser stays open between commands, so each step is one short shell call. ## Install ```bash npm install -g agent-browser agent-browser install # download Chrome for Testing (first time only) ``` - **Homebrew:** `brew install agent-browser`, then `agent-browser install`. - **Linux:** `agent-browser install --with-deps` also installs the browser's system libraries. - **No install:** `npx agent-browser open example.com`. Project installs, building from source, `upgrade`, and `doctor` are covered in [Installation](https://agent-browser.dev/installation).

### Upgrade note: instance-wide settings need a super admin

Provider credentials (such as Plaid), the shared AI connection settings (LLM provider, endpoints, API keys and models), sync settings, and the external assistant connection are stored once for the whole instance and apply to every family. On an instance with more than one family, only a `super_admin` can change them. When there is a single family, its admins keep access. Family-scoped choices, such as which assistant a family uses, stay with that family's admins.

Installs created before the first user was automatically made `super_admin` may have no super admin at all. If your instance has more than one family (for example, because someone else signed up), these instance-wide settings are hidden after the update and saving them returns "not authorized". Promote your own user once:

```bash
docker compose exec web bin/rails runner 'User.find_by!(email: "you@example.com").update!(role: :super_admin)'
```

After that, you can promote other users at `/admin/users`. See section 3.5 of the [OIDC guide](oidc.md) for the console variant.

> **Breaking change (v7.3.0):** `ha_config_set_yaml` has been moved to [beta](docs/beta.md).
### Other install methods These run the server outside Home Assistant — useful for **Container** / **Core** installs (which can't run apps) or a separate host. The [Setup Wizard](https://homeassistant-ai.github.io/ha-mcp/setup/) generates the exact client-specific config for each. - **Docker (HTTP server):** run `ghcr.io/homeassistant-ai/ha-mcp` in HTTP mode, pointed at your Home Assistant URL and a long-lived token (an administrator's is recommended; non-admin tokens work with limitations), and connect your client to its secret URL. See the [Setup Wizard](https://homeassistant-ai.github.io/ha-mcp/setup/) for the full command and per-client config. - **PyPI / uvx (HTTP server):** run the published `ha-mcp` package with `uvx --python 3.14 ha-mcp@latest` (or pip) as a streamable-HTTP server the same way. Details in the [Setup Wizard](https://homeassistant-ai.github.io/ha-mcp/setup/). - **Local stdio (not recommended):** runs ha-mcp on your own machine over stdio. The one-command installers in the **Demo server** section below use this path; the [Setup Wizard](https://homeassistant-ai.github.io/ha-mcp/setup/) covers connecting it to your own Home Assistant. - **OIDC authentication:** gate remote access behind an external identity provider (Authentik, Keycloak, Auth0, etc.) instead of a secret URL — all authenticated users share the server's Home Assistant credentials. See [OIDC Mode](docs/oidc.md). > ⚠️ **stdio has known transport issues.** The stdio transport has connection problems that streamable HTTP does not ([#1713](https://github.com/homeassistant-ai/ha-mcp/issues/1713)). It is recommended only for demo/testing tinkering — for a real setup, use the custom component or an HTTP method above.
🌐 Remote access (Nabu Casa / Webhook Proxy app / OpenAI Tunnel) > **Using the HA-MCP custom component?** You do not need the **Webhook Proxy** — the component has its own built-in webhook for remote access (see the **Get Started** quick start at the top). The proxy is for the **app** (it can also front another external server via its `mcp_server_url` option). The **OpenAI Tunnel** below is different: it applies to **any** install method when Home Assistant isn't publicly reachable at all (no Nabu Casa or reverse proxy). Already have **Nabu Casa** or another reverse proxy pointing at your Home Assistant? The Webhook Proxy app routes MCP traffic through your existing setup — no separate tunnel or port forwarding needed. 1. Install the **MCP Server app** (see above) and the **Webhook Proxy** app from the same store 2. Start the webhook proxy and **restart Home Assistant** when prompted 3. Copy the webhook URL from the app logs: ``` MCP Server URL (remote): https://xxxxx.ui.nabu.casa/api/webhook/mcp_xxxxxxxx ``` 4. Configure your AI client with that URL For other remote access methods (Cloudflare Tunnel, custom reverse proxy), see the [Setup Wizard](https://homeassistant-ai.github.io/ha-mcp/setup/). **ChatGPT / Codex behind a firewall (OpenAI Tunnel).** ChatGPT connectors normally require a publicly reachable URL. If you can't (or don't want to) expose one, the community [OpenAI Tunnel for HA-MCP](https://github.com/norpol/hass-codex-tunnel-mcp) integration by [@norpol](https://github.com/norpol) runs OpenAI's [`tunnel-client`](https://github.com/openai/tunnel-client) inside Home Assistant and connects your local MCP server URL to an OpenAI-hosted tunnel over an outbound-only connection — no port forwarding, reverse proxy, or public URL. Point it at your ha-mcp URL, then attach the ChatGPT connector to the same tunnel ID. See the [FAQ entry](https://homeassistant-ai.github.io/ha-mcp/faq/#openai-tunnel) and [#1811](https://github.com/homeassistant-ai/ha-mcp/issues/1811). [Webhook proxy documentation →](https://github.com/homeassistant-ai/ha-mcp/blob/master/homeassistant-addon-webhook-proxy/DOCS.md)

## Quick start

Requires Node.js 22.13.0+ within 22.x, or Node.js 24.x or 26.x, and Python 3.10+.
Python 3.10 also requires `tomli`.

Install the CLI globally and sign in:

```bash
npm install --global @openai/codex-security
cs login
```

Run your first scan from the repository directory:

```bash
cs scan .
```

When the scan completes, open the Markdown file at the **REPORT** path in the
terminal. Run `cs scans show` from the same repository to find its latest
completed scan again. See [scan scope and follow-up work](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#understand-scan-scope-and-follow-up-work)
for how to interpret exclusions in the report.

`cs` and `codex-security` run the same CLI. If the short name conflicts with
another command, use `codex-security`. To skip the global install, or if npm
reports an `EEXIST` conflict, use `npx @openai/codex-security` in place of
`cs` for both login and scanning.

For CI, set `OPENAI_API_KEY` or `CODEX_API_KEY` in the scan process's environment.
For a headless machine, see [device or SSH login](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#authentication).

### All algorithms are implemented in Java (for educational purposes)
These implementations are intended for learning purposes. As such, they may be less efficient than the Java standard library.

## Quickstart

This runs Auto-Ontology with Docker Compose against Wide World Importers,
Microsoft's sample sales database. You need Docker with Compose v2,
[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), and an NVIDIA API key (`nvapi-...`) from
[build.nvidia.com](https://build.nvidia.com).

1. Clone the repository and create `.env`:

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git && cd auto-ontology
   cp .env.example .env
   ```

   Then set these values in `.env`:

   ```dotenv
   DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY=nvapi-...
   AUTH_SECRET=<a long random string, e.g. from openssl rand -base64 32>
   APP_URL=http://localhost:3000
   POSTGRES_PASSWORD=<a new password>
   CONNECTION_STRINGS=postgresql://postgres:<the same password>@postgres:5432/wideworldimporters
   AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=<a new password>
   PGADMIN_PASSWORD=<a new password>
   ```

   Compose publishes Postgres, pgAdmin, and the web app on the host, so replace
   each default password before you start it. `.env.example` also sets an API
   key per model role: replace each `nvapi-your-api-key-here` with your key, or
   delete those lines so they fall back to `DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY`.

2. Start Postgres and load the sample database. The seed script lives in
   auto-ontology-eval; pass it the Postgres password you set:

   ```bash
   docker compose up -d --wait postgres
   git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology-eval.git ../auto-ontology-eval
   (cd ../auto-ontology-eval && uv sync && cp .env.example .env && \
     POSTGRES_PASSWORD='<the same password>' \
     uv run python scripts/seed/seed_wwi.py --database-name wideworldimporters --drop)
   ```

3. Build and start the rest of the stack:

   ```bash
   docker compose up -d --build
   ```

4. Open <http://localhost:3000> and sign in with `AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_EMAIL` and
   `AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD` from `.env`. Go to **Settings → Semantic
   Compilation** and turn it on. Ingestion runs at startup; compilation starts
   immediately and reports **Semantic compilation is ready** when it finishes.

5. Ask a question in **Chat**:

   > What was revenue for the USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania
   > in June 2015?

   The agent resolves *revenue*, *product*, and *state* to terms in the
   ontology, follows their relationships to the joins it needs, and runs the
   query. The answer comes back with its SQL and the steps that produced it,
   so you can check the result against the source:

   ```text
   Answer:  Revenue for USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania in
            June 2015 was $588.80, from 3 invoice lines.

   SQL:     SELECT SUM(il.extendedprice) AS revenue, COUNT(*) AS invoice_lines
            FROM sales.invoicelines il
            JOIN sales.invoices i             ON il.invoiceid = i.invoiceid
            JOIN warehouse.stockitems si      ON il.stockitemid = si.stockitemid
            JOIN sales.customers c            ON i.customerid = c.customerid
            JOIN application.cities ct        ON c.deliverycityid = ct.cityid
            JOIN application.stateprovinces sp ON ct.stateprovinceid = sp.stateprovinceid
            WHERE si.stockitemname = 'USB food flash drive - sushi roll'
              AND sp.stateprovincename = 'Pennsylvania'
              AND i.invoicedate >= '2015-06-01' AND i.invoicedate < '2015-07-01'

   Steps:   Resolved terms: Invoice Line (revenue), Stock Item, State Province, Invoice
            Joined: invoice line -> invoice -> customer -> city -> state province
            Validated the filter values against the data, then executed
   ```

6. Ask something the data can't answer. Wide World Importers has no
   advertising data, so a question about ad spend has nothing to resolve
   against. An agent connected through [MCP](#mcp-server) checks answerability
   first and asks you to clarify:

   ```text
   You:    What was return on ad spend for the sushi roll flash drive in June 2015?
   Agent:  check_answerable -> coverage 0.5; no term covers "ad spend"
   Agent:  I can find revenue for that product, but this data has no
           advertising spend, so I can't compute return on ad spend. Do you
           want June 2015 revenue instead, or is ad spend tracked in another
           source I should connect?
   ```

If the UI loads without its left navigation after a restart, the browser is
holding a stale session cookie. Clear site data for `localhost:3000` and sign in
again. For other setup failures, see the
[setup skill's troubleshooting guide](./skills/nvidia-ontology-setup/references/troubleshooting.md).


### Models

Auto-Ontology uses four model roles. With an `nvapi-` key, each defaults to an
NVIDIA NIM on [build.nvidia.com](https://build.nvidia.com):

| Role            | Default model                           | What it does                                                                                                                   |
| --------------- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `REASONING`     | `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b` | Builds the ontology (terms, relationships, SQL attributes), writes each answer's SQL and explanation, and grades answerability |
| `NON_REASONING` | `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b` | Runs the agent's faster steps: question intent, entity extraction, candidate selection, and SQL checks and repair              |
| `EMBED`         | `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-embed-1b`          | Indexes tables, columns, terms, and SQL attributes in pgvector, and matches each question to them                              |
| `RERANK`        | `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-rerank-8b`         | Ranks candidate tables when compilation builds bridge-table SQL attributes                                                     |

To use self-hosted NIM or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, set
`<ROLE>_ENDPOINT`, `<ROLE>_API_KEY`, and `<ROLE>_MODEL`. Any field you leave
unset falls back to `DEFAULT_MODELS_<FIELD>`, so the simplest setup fills in
`DEFAULT_MODELS_*` and overrides only what differs. Use models
that support structured output, and keep the embedding model the same for
ingestion and queries. [`.env.example`](./.env.example) documents every
variable.

Your coding agent forgets everything between sessions. Claude-Mem remembers for it.


Quick Start • How It Works • Search Tools • Documentation • Configuration • Troubleshooting • License

Every new session, your agent starts from zero. It re-reads the same files, re-asks the same questions, and walks back into mistakes you already fixed together.

Claude-Mem runs a second agent beside it that takes notes while it works. The next session starts with a short index of what matters, and pulls in the details only when it needs them. Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode and 11 more agents. Copilot CLI, Goose, Roo Code and Warp can search your memory, but their sessions aren't recorded.

## Worktrunk makes git worktrees as easy as branches Worktrees are addressed by branch name; paths are computed from a configurable template. Commands that take a branch also accept the path of the worktree it is checked out in.

Start with the core commands

**Core commands:**
Task Worktrunk Plain git
Switch worktrees wt switch feat cd ../repo.feat
Create + start Claude wt switch -c -x claude feat 
git worktree add -b feat ../repo.feat && \
cd ../repo.feat && \
claude
Clean up wt remove 
cd ../repo && \
git worktree remove ../repo.feat && \
git branch -d feat
List with status wt list git worktree list (paths only)

Expand into the more advanced commands as needed

Workflow automation:

- **[Hooks](https://worktrunk.dev/hook/)** — run commands on create, pre-merge, post-merge, etc - **[LLM commit messages](https://worktrunk.dev/llm-commits/)** — generate commit messages from diffs - **[Merge workflow](https://worktrunk.dev/merge/)** — squash, rebase, merge, clean up in one command - **[Interactive picker](https://worktrunk.dev/switch/#interactive-picker)** — browse worktrees with streaming CI status and diff, log, PR and comment previews - **[Share build caches](https://worktrunk.dev/step/#wt-step-copy-ignored)** — ten worktrees get `target/`, `node_modules/`, etc without building or copying them (on APFS, btrfs, and XFS) - **[`wt list --full`](https://worktrunk.dev/list/#full-mode)** — [CI status](https://worktrunk.dev/list/#ci-status) and [AI-generated summaries](https://worktrunk.dev/list/#llm-summaries) per branch - **[PR checkout](https://worktrunk.dev/switch/#pull-requests-and-merge-requests)** — `wt switch pr:123` to jump straight to a PR's branch - **[Dev server per worktree](https://worktrunk.dev/tips-patterns/#dev-server-per-worktree)** — `hash_port` template filter gives each worktree a unique port - **[Aliases](https://worktrunk.dev/extending/#aliases) & [per-branch variables](https://worktrunk.dev/config/#wt-config-state-vars)** — custom `wt ` commands and branch-scoped state for hook templates - ...and **[lots more](#next-steps)** Multiple parallel agents, same simple commands: ![Worktrunk omnibus demo: multiple Claude agents in Zellij tabs with hooks, LLM commits, and merge workflow](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/max-sixty/worktrunk-assets/main/assets/docs/light/wt-zellij-omnibus.gif)

## Recalculate (mandatory whenever the file contains formulas)

openpyxl writes formulas as strings with **no cached values**. Until you recalculate, every
formula cell reads back as `None` to anything reading cached values — `pandas`,
`load_workbook(data_only=True)`, and most previewers.

```bash
python scripts/recalc.py output.xlsx [timeout_seconds]   # default 30
```

LibreOffice computes every formula, the file is **rewritten in place**, and you get JSON:
`status` (`success` | `errors_found`), `total_formulas`, `total_errors`, and an
`error_summary` naming up to 100 cells per error type (`locations_truncated` says how many it
withheld — trust `total_errors`, not the length of the list). Fix what it names and run it
again. **JSON with an `error` key instead of a `status` means nothing was recalculated**, and
only that case exits non-zero — `errors_found` exits 0, so never treat a clean exit as a clean
workbook.

**A green recalc proves your formulas *evaluate*, not that they are *right*.** An off-by-one
range or a reference to the wrong row yields a clean, error-free file with wrong numbers.
Write 2–3 formulas first and check they pull the values you expect, before building out a grid.

**A workbook that links to another file loses those links** if you re-save it with openpyxl and
then recalculate. Such a formula reads `='[1]Returns Analysis'!$B$2` — the `[1]` is an index
into the workbook's external-reference list, naming a *separate file on disk*, not a sheet.
That file is rarely present here, so the cell's cached value is the only thing holding its
data. openpyxl strips that value on save; LibreOffice then has to resolve the reference for
real, fails, writes `#NAME?`, and deletes every link. `recalc.py` refuses to run in that state
— copy those cells' values out of the original before you save over them (`--force` overrides,
and accepts the loss).

### Prerequisites

- [Git](https://git-scm.com/)
- [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup) — the native installer is recommended (`npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code` also works, on Node.js 22+)
- [Python 3](https://www.python.org/) — reads `project.yaml` for every skill and hook; without it every setting silently falls back to its default
- Bash — runs every hook; built into macOS and Linux, and on Windows it comes with [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/downloads/win). Without it on Windows the hooks skip themselves, and session start says their checks are off
- **Chrome, Edge or Chromium** — `/prototype` plays and screenshots each game in it; without one, those checks say they were not assessed
- **Recommended**: [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) (to grow a game into a web project, for a 3D game's three.js, and for the web engine's build and tests) and [jq](https://jqlang.github.io/jq/) (for hook validation)

Hooks fail gracefully if optional tools are missing — you just lose validation — with one deliberate exception: a commit that stages data JSON is blocked when there is no Python to validate it.

## Command line

```bash
curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, in PowerShell:

```powershell
irm https://t3.codes/install.ps1 | iex
```

This installs the `t3` binary to `~/.local/bin`. If that folder is not on your
`PATH` yet, the installer says so and, for zsh, bash on Linux, and fish, prints
a command to add it. On Windows, `t3` works in the same PowerShell window right
away; add the folder to your `PATH` for new windows. If a `t3` that the
installer or the desktop app did not create is already there, it leaves that
one alone and stops. Set `T3CODE_CHANNEL=nightly` to install the nightly train, or
`T3CODE_VERSION` to pin an exact version.

| Task                                  | Command                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Start the server and open the web app | `t3`                                                                    |
| Start the server without a browser    | `t3 serve`                                                              |
| Use it from your other devices        | `t3 up` ([details](./remote-access.md))                                 |
| Keep it running in the background     | `t3 service install` ([details](./background-service.md))               |
| Move to the newest release            | `t3 update`                                                             |
| Reclaim database space                | `t3 doctor` ([details](./background-service.md#reclaim-database-space)) |
| Remove it again                       | `t3 uninstall`                                                          |

Run `t3 help` or `t3 --help` for the full reference. To start in a new working
directory, use an explicit path such as `t3 ./my-project`. A bare directory name
is accepted only if it already exists.

If `t3` or `t3 start` reports an already running server, connect to that server
instead. Stop it before starting a replacement, or use a different `--base-dir`
for an independent server.

To try T3 Code once without installing it, run `npx t3@latest` instead (needs
Node.js for `npx`). It offers to install the `t3` command first. If you say no,
it asks again at the next minor release, and `npx t3 install` installs it later.
`npx t3` always runs the version npm picked, even when a `t3` is installed. On
the nightly train, run your installed `t3` (for example `t3 connect`), not
`npx t3`, which runs the latest stable release.

# Hallmark **A design skill for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode that refuses to look AI-generated.** [usehallmark.com](https://www.usehallmark.com)  ·  fifty themes  ·  custom on request  ·  redesign and audit by name Made by Together AI.

Hallmark holds a hard floor and then gets out of the way. It deals three themes from a catalog of fifty materials, builds the page around what the visitor came to do, and lints the result in a real browser against the tells that read as machine-made: the eyebrow above every heading, tracked-capital labels, one coloured word in a headline, a page of empty frames or nothing but photographs, a hero that misses its screen, an email sign-up at the end of every page, a form that says thanks without sending anything. A fresh-context reviewer gets the last word. The gates come in tiers. The **Floor** never ships (contrast, focus, reduced motion, invented facts, a broken phone layout). **Reflex** gates are the defaults a model falls into; a build with a reason may overrule one on the record. **Finish** checks are craft detail that never blocks a ship. ## Install ``` npx skills add nutlope/hallmark -g ``` `-g` installs for every project; leave it off to install into the current one. Needs Node 18 or later. The browser checks (`sloplint --render`, screenshots) also need `npm i -g puppeteer-core` and Chrome; without them the static checks still run. | Harness | Lands in | Invoke | | --- | --- | --- | | Claude Code | `~/.claude/skills/hallmark` | `/hallmark ` or describe a new build | | Codex CLI | `~/.agents/skills/hallmark` | `$hallmark ` or describe a new build | | Cursor | finds the copies above | `/hallmark ` or describe a new build | | OpenCode | finds the copies above | `/hallmark ` or describe a new build | - **One harness only:** `npx skills add nutlope/hallmark -g --agent claude-code` (or `codex`, `opencode`, `cursor`, `github-copilot`). - **As a Claude Code plugin:** `/plugin marketplace add nutlope/hallmark`, then `/plugin install hallmark@hallmark` (invoked as `/hallmark:hallmark`). - **From a clone:** `node skills/hallmark/scripts/install.mjs` validates every theme and reference before it copies; `install-hook.mjs` adds an edit-time Floor check to Claude Code. - **Lint any page:** `node skills/hallmark/scripts/sloplint.mjs --render`. - **If it does not fire on its own,** name it: *use hallmark to build ...*.

## Requirements

- A coding agent with a model that supports tool use and parallel sub-agents
- Node.js for the zero-dependency findings and coverage-ledger validators
- An OS-enforced sandbox for target-controlled builds, tests, processes, browsers, emulators, fuzzers, and fixtures. It must disable external networking, use a sanitized allowlisted environment, enforce resource limits, and allow writes only to assigned scratch paths. Without these controls, the workflow keeps the lead as `needs_validation` instead of executing target code.

## Skills

HyperFrames ships 9 skills. Make any video by asking for it; the `/hyperframes` skill carries the contract and the references (film, captions, overlays, motion, look). Read it first.

For standalone installation, default to the **core set** (`/hyperframes`, `/hyperframes-cli`, `/hyperframes-registry`, `/media-use`, `/reverse-any-video`, `/style-sampling`). `npx hyperframes skills update` installs exactly that from anywhere; the interactive picker (`npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes`) lists it as the "Core Skills" group, nothing pre-selected. The picker is interactive-only — a non-interactive or agent run without `--skill` installs all 9. Use `npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes --all` to install the complete published set deliberately (skips the picker), or `npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes --skill <name>` for just one (bare name, no leading `/`).

Standalone installs stay lean after that: `npx hyperframes init` installs the **core set** only when it is missing and never touches a skill you already have (`npx hyperframes skills update` refreshes them, and never removes one); `/figma`, `/slideshow` and `/remotion-to-hyperframes` install **on demand** with `npx hyperframes skills update <name>`. Nothing re-pulls the full set behind your back.


### Manually with the CLI

```bash
npx hyperframes init my-video
cd my-video
npx hyperframes preview      # preview in browser with live reload
npx hyperframes render       # render to MP4
```

**Requirements:** Node.js 22+, FFmpeg

## What's new in 2.0

- **From 9 to 36 skills.** New skills cover deal reviews, close plans, stakeholder maps, renewals, customer health, lead routing, CRM updates, meeting booking, inbox sweeps and team pipeline views.
- **Works across CRMs and email providers.** Skills read your CRM's own stages and fields instead of assuming one vendor's setup, and work the same on Gmail or Outlook, Slack or Teams. No settings file is needed; a skill asks once for anything it cannot find.
- **Uses uploaded files when nothing is connected.** Upload a pipeline export, a transcript or a list of accounts, and the skill works from that.
- **Acts when you ask.** Skills can update CRM records, create email drafts or send email, post to chat and book meetings, within each connector's permissions. Changes a skill suggests on its own are shown to you first, with the evidence behind them.
- **Treats outside content as information.** Emails, call transcripts, chat messages and documents are read as information, never as instructions. If an email or transcript asks for an action, the skill shows you the action before anything happens.
- **Existing skill names still work.** `account-research`, `call-summary`, `forecast`, `call-prep`, `daily-briefing`, `draft-outreach`, `pipeline-review`, `competitive-intelligence` and `create-an-asset` keep their names, rebuilt on the new skills. Two behave differently: `create-an-asset` now builds decks, one-pagers and leave-behinds from your account data rather than landing pages or interactive demos, and `forecast` writes a commit, best-case and pipeline narrative instead of best, likely and worst scenarios.

# VoiceStudio — Install on macOS

VoiceStudio's macOS desktop app is built with Electron. The archived Tauri app
is no longer maintained; if you still run it, follow the
[migration guide](../electron-migration.md).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Intel Macs are not supported** for the local backend (app UI only).
> PyTorch stopped shipping Intel-Mac (macOS
> x86_64) wheels after 2.2.x and VoiceStudio's dependencies need a newer torch,
> so a local Python backend cannot install on an Intel Mac — from the DMG *or*
> from source ([#889](https://github.com/debpalash/VoiceStudio/issues/889)).
> On Intel, packaged setup stops before creating a Python environment or
> downloading dependencies and shows remote-backend guidance instead: use the
> remote connection controls on the setup screen to point the app at a backend
> on another machine, or run VoiceStudio on an Apple Silicon Mac, Windows, or
> Linux. A source checkout behaves the same way: `bun run setup:api` stops
> before syncing anything, and the app opens the same remote-backend screen
> instead of reporting an incomplete Python environment
> ([#3584](https://github.com/debpalash/VoiceStudio/issues/3584)).

### Live mode

`/impeccable live` opens your running dev server with an overlay. Select an element, pick a direction, and Impeccable hot-swaps variants in place. Accept one and it is written back to your source. It works with Vite, Next, SvelteKit, Astro, Nuxt, and plain HTML. [Iterate in the browser](https://impeccable.style/tutorials/iterate-live).

Live mode edits a local checkout only; don't inject it into a deployed site or weaken a production CSP to make it work. Applying copy edits runs your `package.json`'s optional `impeccable:manual-edit-validate` script with your permissions, so review it before using live mode in an unfamiliar repo.

Apply sends staged copy edits to your chat agent while a live session is polling. If none has polled in the last minute, it runs the `codex` CLI from your PATH instead (or `claude` when codex is missing), with approvals, permission checks, and sandboxing off (`--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` or `--permission-mode bypassPermissions`) and your environment inherited. Its prompt carries the staged edits, the edited elements' HTML and nearby text, the page URL, and candidate source paths. Set `IMPECCABLE_LIVE_COPY_AGENT=chat` in the environment that starts live mode to keep Apply in your chat session, or `off` to disable Apply. The server reads it once at startup.
